title: Your agent is blindfolded — Johan Lajili, Poolside AI

primary.label: Coding Agents & Software Engineering

summary: Johan Lajili of Poolside AI opens by noting the stark divergence in developer experiences with AI coding agents—some report near-total automation while others call the output garbage. He dismisses common explanations (the person is a shill, didn't try it, or greenfield-vs-brownfield matters), noting he and others have used AI successfully on legacy code. The real differentiator, he argues, is the feedback loop. In greenfield work, the agent's intuition about how components interact is correct. In brownfield work, unexpected dead ends, unused code, and hidden dependencies violate that intuition. When agents say a feature works, they mean it should work to the best of their knowledge—whether or not they could verify it. This gap erodes trust, especially for skeptics who give up rather than iterate. Lajili presents a CLI tool called "Spoolside" that gives agents visibility: screenshots, token-compressed snapshots, backend and frontend logs, service restarts, and high-level navigation commands. This lets agents reproduce bugs before fixing them, which he considers the first step to trust—without it, he must manually verify work, wasting time and precluding overnight autonomous operation. He frames engineers' evolving role as shifting from product features to building AI scaffolding: tools (as CLIs, skills, or MCPs), codebase improvements, and knowledge bases. He calls this the "AIX engineer" role. Using an airline oxygen-mask analogy, he urges investing in AI self-service before features. In Q&A, Lajili explains he prefers ephemeral human-like testing over rigid automated tests, recommends stepping back when an agent misses issues to build tooling for self-discovery, and suggests reviewing agent logs for "stinks" like excessive sleep calls. He stresses tooling must fit the specific product context.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: The gap between successful and failed AI coding experiences is the feedback loop, not greenfield vs. brownfield
Agents claiming "it works" really mean "it should work to the best of my knowledge"—verification capability is the trust determinant
Agents should reproduce bugs before fixing them; without that, manual verification destroys the productivity gains
Build your own tooling (CLI, skill, or MCP) to let agents see, navigate, and test your specific application
Engineers' role is shifting from building product features to making AI effective on the product—"AIX engineers"
Invest in AI self-service before features, like putting your own oxygen mask on first
Review agent logs for "stinks" (e.g., excessive sleep calls, repeated storybook runs) as a debugging loop
Tailor feedback tooling to your product context—permissions, 3D worlds, UI layout all demand different approaches

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Johan Lajili introduces himself as being from Poolside, a company building foundational models and coding agents from scratch.

sections.title: Divergent AI experiences
sections.summary: Lajili observes that developers report vastly different AI experiences—from total automation to garbage output—and lists common but unsatisfying explanations (shilling, lying, greenfield vs. brownfield).

sections.title: Feedback loop is the real differentiator
sections.summary: He argues the greenfield-brownfield distinction is really about feedback loops. In greenfield, agent intuition is correct; in brownfield, dead ends and hidden dependencies violate it. Agents claiming success mean it should work given what they know, not that they verified it.

sections.title: Spoolside CLI tool
sections.summary: Lajili presents Spoolside, a CLI tool giving agents screenshots, snapshots, logs, service restarts, and navigation commands for his VS Code extension product. This lets agents reproduce bugs before fixing them, which is the first step to trust.

sections.title: The AIX engineer role
sections.summary: Engineers must shift from product features to making AI effective on the product via tools, codebase improvements, and knowledge bases. This is the emerging AIX engineer role. Lajili uses the airline oxygen-mask analogy: serve the AI before features.

sections.title: Q&A: testing philosophy and patterns
sections.summary: Lajili prefers ephemeral human-like testing over rigid automated tests, recommends building tooling so agents self-discover issues, suggests reviewing logs for stinks like excessive sleep calls, and stresses tailoring tooling to the specific product context.

demonstrations: Spoolside CLI tool captures screenshots and token-compressed snapshots of a VS Code extension
Log extraction from backend and frontend services with high-level navigation and messaging commands
Bug reproduction workflow where agents verify issues before attempting fixes
limitations: Spoolside is not publicly available on GitHub—it is an example to inspire building your own tooling
Automated tests can be too rigid and hard to maintain over time
